note: Read scribe.json for what a claim is and how it is rated. Each claim has a sample of its own, holding only the rows that claim is about. They used to share one, and a claim's signal then included a total that moved when a DIFFERENT claim broke, so a correct total read as a broken one. A claim-by-claim audit needs claims that can each be wrong on their own. Two claims are probed against the weekly summary, because the record states them without qualifying which summary it means and the recorded change made the two disagree. C6 is the planted one: the two summaries are SUPPOSED to differ — a month answers what was spent in January, a week is read beside the bank's statement — so the claim is that each follows the date its own setting names, not that they agree.

claims.policy: money moved between your own accounts
claims.statement: Money moved between your own accounts is left out of the totals.

probe.present_means: the total is the one purchase alone, with both transfer legs outside it
probe.absent_means: the total has moved, so money between your own accounts is being counted as spending

claims.statement: A row recorded twice is counted once, matched on its date, its amount and its merchant.

probe.present_means: a coffee and a pastry of the same amount on the same day are both counted in the weekly summary as well, so the match uses the merchant everywhere
probe.absent_means: the weekly summary merges two different merchants of the same amount on one day, so the record's unqualified claim is true of the monthly summary only

claims.policy: which month a transaction counts in
claims.statement: A transaction counts in the month it was made, not the month the bank posted it.

probe.present_means: a transaction made in January and posted in February counts in January
probe.absent_means: it counts in the month the bank posted it instead

claims.statement: A payment whose merchant matches no rule is printed as an uncategorised row among the other categories, so the rows a reader can see add up to the total printed underneath them.

probe.present_means: the bucket is printed as a row of its own, so the visible figures account for the total
probe.absent_means: the bucket is counted in the total and in the count line at the end but has no row, so the visible figures come to less than the total and the difference is the unmatched money
probe.note: The signal is the whole row including its spacing, not the word on its own, because the count line at the end of the run also contains the word uncategorised and would make a missing row read as a row that is there.

claims.statement: A refund is netted against its own category rather than reported separately.

probe.present_means: the refund is netted against groceries
probe.absent_means: the refund is not netted against groceries

claims.policy: which date each summary is lined up on
claims.statement: Each summary is lined up on the date its own setting names, so the weekly one follows the date the bank posted a payment.

probe.present_means: the weekly summary buckets by the date the payment was MADE, so `week = "posted"` in rules.toml was read, validated and had no effect — both summaries were handed the month's date
probe.absent_means: the week follows the posting date its setting names, so it reads next to the statement the bank sends
